title: Αἰετὸς καὶ δράκων
titleEn: The Eagle and the Serpent — Iliad 12.182–276
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Polypoetes and Leonteus cut down a string of victims, while Hector and Polydamas, with the main force of Trojan young men, still hesitate at the ditch. An eagle flying on their left, carrying a living serpent, is bitten by it, drops it among the Trojans and screams away on the wind. Polydamas reads the sign as a warning: if the Trojans break the wall they will lose many men on the way back, and he advises against the attack. Hector answers in anger. He trusts the plans of Zeus, not birds, says the one good omen is to fight for one’s country, and threatens Polydamas with death if he holds back. Zeus then raises a storm-wind that blows dust at the ships and gives glory to Hector, and the Trojans tear at the battlements and pillars of the wall, while the two Ajaxes go along the towers, rebuking and urging the Achaeans.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ αὖ Πειριθόου υἱὸς κρατερὸς Πολυποίτης
δουρὶ βάλεν Δάμασον κυνέης διὰ χαλκοπαρῄου·
sentences.tr:
enth’ au Peirithoou huios krateros Polypoitēs
douri balen Damason kyneēs dia chalkoparēiou·
sentences.l:
Then in turn Peirithous’ son, strong Polypoetes,
with a spear struck Damasus through the bronze-cheeked helmet;
sentences.i: Then in turn strong Polypoetes, the son of Peirithous, struck Damasus with his spear through his bronze-cheeked helmet;
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ αὖ ‘then in turn’ takes the fighting up where the last part left it, with the Lapiths. Πειριθόου is the genitive of Πειρίθοος, so ‘Peirithous’ son’ gives the father’s name; κρατερός is ‘strong’. δουρί (dative of δόρυ) is the spear he strikes with, and βάλεν is the aorist of βάλλω without its augment. κυνέης ‘helmet’ is the genitive after διά ‘through’, and χαλκοπαρῄου ‘bronze-cheeked’ goes with it (the cheek-pieces are the likely reference).

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρα χαλκείη κόρυς ἔσχεθεν, ἀλλὰ διὰ πρὸ
αἰχμὴ χαλκείη ῥῆξ’ ὀστέον, ἐγκέφαλος δὲ
ἔνδον ἅπας πεπάλακτο·
sentences.tr:
oud’ ara chalkeiē korys eschethen, alla dia pro
aichmē chalkeiē rhēx’ osteon, enkephalos de
endon hapas pepalakto·
sentences.i: and the bronze helmet did not hold out: the bronze point drove right through and broke the bone, and all the brain inside was spattered about;
sentences.n: The subject of οὐδ’ ἔσχεθεν is the helmet, κόρυς: ἔσχεθεν is a poetic aorist of ἔχω, here ‘held out’, held off the blow. διὰ πρό is ‘right through’, printed as two words. αἰχμή is the spear’s point, and ῥῆξ’ is ῥῆξε, from ῥήγνυμι ‘break’. πεπάλακτο is the pluperfect passive of παλάσσω ‘spatter’, without its augment; its subject is ἐγκέφαλος ‘brain’, and ἅπας ‘all of it’ agrees with it.

sentences.t: δάμασσε δέ μιν μεμαῶτα·
sentences.tr: damasse de min memaōta·
sentences.l: and he subdued him, eager as he was.
sentences.i: and so he overcame him as he charged.
sentences.n: The subject is still Polypoetes. δάμασσε is ἐδάμασσε without its augment, from δαμάζω ‘subdue’, and it shares its root with the victim’s name Δάμασος, so the verb seems to play on it. μιν is the old pronoun ‘him’ (accusative); μεμαῶτα ‘eager’, a participle of μέμαα, agrees with it.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα Πύλωνα καὶ Ὄρμενον ἐξενάριξεν.
sentences.tr: autar epeita Pylōna kai Ormenon exenarixen.
sentences.l: and then Pylon and Ormenus he despoiled.
sentences.i: And after that he killed Pylon and Ormenus and stripped them of their armour.
sentences.n: Still Polypoetes. ἐξενάριξεν (from ἐξεναρίζω) means to kill a man and strip his armour, so both are in the one verb; ἐνάρα is the spoils. Πύλωνα and Ὄρμενον are accusatives of the names Πύλων and Ὄρμενος. αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα ‘and then’ is a stock way of moving to the next victim.

sentences.t:
υἱὸν δ’ Ἀντιμάχοιο Λεοντεὺς ὄζος Ἄρηος
Ἱππόμαχον βάλε δουρὶ κατὰ ζωστῆρα τυχήσας.
sentences.tr:
huion d’ Antimachoio Leonteus ozos Arēos
Hippomachon bale douri kata zōstēra tychēsas.
sentences.l:
As for the son of Antimachus, Leonteus, scion of Ares,
Hippomachus he struck with a spear, hitting him at the belt.
sentences.i: Leonteus, scion of Ares, struck Hippomachus, the son of Antimachus, with his spear, hitting him at the belt.
sentences.n: The Greek opens with the victim: υἱὸν … Ἀντιμάχοιο ‘the son of Antimachus’ is the object, and Ἱππόμαχον in the next line names him; the subject, Λεοντεύς, is held back to the last three words of line 188. ὄζος Ἄρηος ‘scion of Ares’ is the title that goes with Leonteus (ὄζος is literally ‘branch’). τυχήσας is the aorist participle of τυγχάνω ‘hit’, with κατὰ ζωστῆρα ‘at the belt’.

sentences.t:
αὖτις δ’ ἐκ κολεοῖο ἐρυσσάμενος ξίφος ὀξὺ
Ἀντιφάτην μὲν πρῶτον ἐπαΐξας δι’ ὁμίλου
πλῆξ’ αὐτοσχεδίην·
sentences.tr:
autis d’ ek koleoio eryssamenos xiphos oxy
Antiphatēn men prōton epaïxas di’ homilou
plēx’ autoschediēn·
sentences.i: Next he drew his sharp sword from its scabbard and, rushing through the throng, struck Antiphates first, at close quarters;
sentences.n: The subject is still Leonteus. αὖτις ‘again’ means ‘next’, after the spear-thrust. κολεοῖο is the epic genitive of κολεός ‘scabbard’; ἐρυσσάμενος (aorist middle participle of ἐρύω) is ‘having drawn’. μὲν πρῶτον ‘first’ is answered by αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα in line 193. ἐπαΐξας is an aorist participle ‘rushing upon’, with δι’ ὁμίλου ‘through the throng’. πλῆξ’ is πλῆξε, from πλήσσω ‘strike’. αὐτοσχεδίην is a feminine accusative used as an adverb, ‘at close quarters’; no noun is stated for it.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ ὕπτιος οὔδει ἐρείσθη·
sentences.tr: ho d’ ar’ hyptios oudei ereisthē·
sentences.l: and he on his back was driven to the ground;
sentences.i: and he was driven down on his back onto the ground;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ ‘and he’ is Antiphates, with the old demonstrative ὅ that is turning into the article. ἐρείσθη is the aorist passive of ἐρείδω ‘press, drive’; ὕπτιος ‘on his back’ agrees with the subject, and οὔδει is the dative of οὖδας ‘ground’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα Μένωνα καὶ Ἰαμενὸν καὶ Ὀρέστην
πάντας ἐπασσυτέρους πέλασε χθονὶ πουλυβοτείρῃ.
sentences.tr:
autar epeita Menōna kai Iamenon kai Orestēn
pantas epassyterous pelase chthoni poulyboteirēi.
sentences.l:
and then Menon and Iamenus and Orestes,
all one close upon another, he brought to the much-nourishing earth.
sentences.i: and then he brought down Menon and Iamenus and Orestes, all one after another, to the earth that feeds so many.
sentences.n: The last line is the formula that closes a list of victims, repeated word for word from an earlier list in the Iliad, and its English is kept. ἐπασσυτέρους is an adjective ‘one close upon another’, agreeing with πάντας. πέλασε is the aorist of πελάζω ‘bring near’. πουλυβοτείρῃ ‘much-nourishing’ is the epic form of πολυβοτείρῃ and goes with χθονί ‘earth’. The subject is Leonteus.

sentences.t:
ὄφρ’ οἳ τοὺς ἐνάριζον ἀπ’ ἔντεα μαρμαίροντα,
τόφρ’ οἳ Πουλυδάμαντι καὶ Ἕκτορι κοῦροι ἕποντο,
sentences.tr:
ophr’ hoi tous enarizon ap’ entea marmaironta,
tophr’ hoi Poulydamanti kai Hektori kouroi heponto,
sentences.l:
While these were despoiling those men, off them the sparkling gear,
meanwhile those, the young men, followed Polydamas and Hector,
sentences.i: While these were stripping the sparkling gear from the dead, the young men were meanwhile following Polydamas and Hector,
sentences.n: ὄφρα … τόφρα ‘while … meanwhile’ ties two scenes together, and each is followed by a demonstrative οἵ, ‘these’ and ‘those’: the victors are stripping the dead while the Trojan young men follow their leaders. ἐνάριζον is the imperfect of ἐναρίζω, ‘strip’ (a slain man); ἀπ’ is the preposition cut loose from it, ‘off’. ἔντεα is ‘gear’, and μαρμαίροντα ‘sparkling’. ἕποντο is the unaugmented imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’; κοῦροι ‘young men’ stands in apposition to the second οἵ.

sentences.t:
οἳ πλεῖστοι καὶ ἄριστοι ἔσαν, μέμασαν δὲ μάλιστα
τεῖχός τε ῥήξειν καὶ ἐνιπρήσειν πυρὶ νῆας,
sentences.tr:
hoi pleistoi kai aristoi esan, memasan de malista
teichos te rhēxein kai eniprēsein pyri nēas,
sentences.l:
who were the most numerous and the best, and were most eager
both to break the wall and to burn the ships with fire,
sentences.i: the largest and the best, and they were keenest of all both to break the wall and to burn the ships with fire,
sentences.n: The relative clause qualifies the young men who follow Polydamas and Hector. The first half of the line, οἳ πλεῖστοι καὶ ἄριστοι ἔσαν, μέμασαν δὲ μάλιστα, is the very line that described Hector’s division at 12.89, so its English is kept. ἔσαν is the epic ἦσαν; μέμασαν is the perfect of μέμαα ‘be eager’, used as a past tense. ῥήξειν and ἐνιπρήσειν are future infinitives (ῥήγνυμι ‘break’, ἐνιπίμπρημι ‘burn’); τε … καὶ means ‘both … and’.

sentences.t: οἵ ῥ’ ἔτι μερμήριζον ἐφεσταότες παρὰ τάφρῳ.
sentences.tr: hoi rh’ eti mermērizon ephestaotes para taphrōi.
sentences.l: who still were in doubt, standing by the ditch.
sentences.i: They were still in doubt between two courses, standing by the ditch.
sentences.n: οἵ ῥ’ is οἵ ῥα, ‘they who’, taking up the same young men a third time. μερμήριζον is the imperfect of μερμηρίζω ‘be in doubt between two courses’, the verb Homer uses when a man weighs them; the course they are weighing is the one Polydamas will put into words. ἐφεσταότες is the perfect participle of ἐφίστημι in its epic form, ‘standing at’, with παρὰ τάφρῳ ‘beside the ditch’.

sentences.t:
ὄρνις γάρ σφιν ἐπῆλθε περησέμεναι μεμαῶσιν
αἰετὸς ὑψιπέτης ἐπ’ ἀριστερὰ λαὸν ἐέργων
φοινήεντα δράκοντα φέρων ὀνύχεσσι πέλωρον
ζωὸν ἔτ’ ἀσπαίροντα, καὶ οὔ πω λήθετο χάρμης,
sentences.tr:
ornis gar sphin epēlthe perēsemenai memaōsin
aietos hypsipetēs ep’ aristera laon eergōn
phoinēenta drakonta pherōn onychessi pelōron
zōon et’ aspaironta, kai ou pō lētheto charmēs,
sentences.l:
For a bird came upon them as they were eager to cross,
a high-flying eagle, on the left keeping the people shut off,
bearing in its talons a blood-red serpent, a monster,
alive, still gasping, and not yet had it forgotten the joy of battle,
sentences.i: For a bird came upon them as they were eager to cross: a high-flying eagle, barring the army’s way on the left, carrying in its talons a blood-red serpent, a monster, still alive and gasping, and not yet forgetful of the joy of battle,
sentences.n: This is the omen itself; Polydamas will repeat it in lines 218–221, almost word for word. ὄρνις ‘bird’ is named first and αἰετός ‘eagle’ follows in apposition. σφιν is the epic dative ‘to them’; περησέμεναι is the future infinitive of περάω ‘cross’ (the ditch), and μεμαῶσιν ‘eager’ agrees with σφιν. ὑψιπέτης ‘high-flying’. ἐπ’ ἀριστερά is ‘on the left’; λαὸν ἐέργων ‘shutting off the army’ does not make clear whether the eagle blocks the way or sweeps across it. φοινήεντα ‘blood-red’ is the usual sense, but the word may suggest slaughter, and it is not certain. πέλωρον is a noun, ‘monster’, not an adjective. ἀσπαίροντα ‘gasping’; the subject of λήθετο ‘forgot’ is the serpent, and it takes the genitive χάρμης ‘joy of battle’.

sentences.t:
κόψε γὰρ αὐτὸν ἔχοντα κατὰ στῆθος παρὰ δειρὴν
ἰδνωθεὶς ὀπίσω·
sentences.tr:
kopse gar auton echonta kata stēthos para deirēn
idnōtheis opisō·
sentences.l:
for it struck him, as he held it, on the breast beside the neck,
having doubled itself backward;
sentences.i: for the serpent struck the eagle that held it, on the breast beside the neck, doubling itself backward;
sentences.n: The subject of κόψε is the serpent, carried over from δράκοντα above; αὐτόν is the eagle, and ἔχοντα ‘holding (it)’ agrees with αὐτόν. κόψε is the aorist of κόπτω ‘strike’, here a bite. ἰδνωθείς (aorist passive participle of ἰδνόομαι ‘bend, double over’) with ὀπίσω ‘backward’ shows the serpent curling back on the eagle.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἀπὸ ἕθεν ἧκε χαμᾶζε
ἀλγήσας ὀδύνῃσι, μέσῳ δ’ ἐνὶ κάββαλ’ ὁμίλῳ,
sentences.tr:
ho d’ apo hethen hēke chamaze
algēsas odynēisi, mesōi d’ eni kabbal’ homilōi,
sentences.l:
and he from himself let it go to the ground,
hurt with pains, and in the midst of the throng cast it down,
sentences.i: and the eagle, smarting with pain, let it fall from him to the ground, and cast it down in the midst of the throng,
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is now the eagle. ἕθεν is the old reflexive pronoun ‘from himself’; ἧκε is the aorist of ἵημι ‘send, let go’. ἀλγήσας ὀδύνῃσι is ‘hurt with pains’ (ἀλγέω, dative plural of ὀδύνη). κάββαλ’ is κατὰ … βάλε run together (tmesis for καταβάλλω), with κατά cut short and assimilated to the β that follows, ‘cast down’; μέσῳ … ὁμίλῳ with ἐνί is ‘in the midst of the throng’.

sentences.t: αὐτὸς δὲ κλάγξας πέτετο πνοιῇς ἀνέμοιο.
sentences.tr: autos de klanxas peteto pnoiēis anemoio.
sentences.l: and himself, having screamed, flew on the breathings of the wind.
sentences.i: and he himself, with a scream, flew off on the breath of the wind.
sentences.n: αὐτὸς δέ ‘and he himself’ sets the eagle against the serpent it has dropped. κλάγξας is the aorist participle of κλάζω ‘scream’. πέτετο is the imperfect of πέτομαι ‘fly’. πνοιῇς is the dative plural of πνοιή ‘breath (of wind)’, with ἀνέμοιο the epic genitive of ἄνεμος.

sentences.t:
Τρῶες δ’ ἐρρίγησαν ὅπως ἴδον αἰόλον ὄφιν
κείμενον ἐν μέσσοισι Διὸς τέρας αἰγιόχοιο.
sentences.tr:
Trōes d’ errigēsan hopōs idon aiolon ophin
keimenon en messoisi Dios teras aigiochoio.
sentences.l:
And the Trojans shuddered when they saw the glancing serpent
lying in their midst, a portent of aegis-bearing Zeus.
sentences.i: The Trojans shuddered when they saw the glancing serpent lying in their midst, a portent of aegis-bearing Zeus.
sentences.n: ἐρρίγησαν is the aorist of ῥιγέω ‘shudder’; line 208 is metrically irregular as transmitted: it scans only if the ι of ἐρρίγησαν is long, and even then its last foot, ὄφιν, begins with a short ὄ where the metre needs a long syllable. ὅπως here is ‘when’. αἰόλος ‘glancing’ is a word whose sense is not known for a serpent (quick-moving, gleaming, or mottled); it is the second half of κορυθαίολος. κείμενον ‘lying’ agrees with ὄφιν, and ἐν μέσσοισι is ‘in the midst’, the epic dative plural. Διὸς τέρας ‘a portent of Zeus’ is in apposition to the serpent; αἰγιόχοιο ‘aegis-bearing’ is a stock epithet, and its meaning is disputed.

sentences.t: δὴ τότε Πουλυδάμας θρασὺν Ἕκτορα εἶπε παραστάς·
sentences.tr: dē tote Poulydamas thrasyn Hektora eipe parastas·
sentences.l: then indeed Polydamas to bold Hector spoke, standing beside him:
sentences.i: Then Polydamas stood beside bold Hector and spoke:
sentences.n: This line introduces Polydamas’ speech, the same line that introduced his earlier speech at 12.60, so its English is kept. δὴ τότε ‘then indeed’; θρασύς is ‘bold’; εἶπε is the aorist of λέγω ‘say’, and παραστάς is the aorist participle of παρίστημι ‘standing beside’.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορ ἀεὶ μέν πώς μοι ἐπιπλήσσεις ἀγορῇσιν
ἐσθλὰ φραζομένῳ,
sentences.tr:
Hektor aei men pōs moi epiplēsseis agorēisin
esthla phrazomenōi,
sentences.l:
“Hector, always, in some way, you chide me in the assemblies,
me planning good things,
sentences.i: “Hector, you are always somehow chiding me in the assemblies when I am planning good things,
sentences.n: Polydamas begins by naming the quarrel: Hector keeps scolding him in the assembly. The vocative Ἕκτορ is recessive in accent. ἀεὶ μέν is answered by νῦν αὖτ’ in 215. πώς is an enclitic ‘somehow’. ἐπιπλήσσεις (from ἐπιπλήσσω ‘chide’) takes the dative μοι; ἀγορῇσιν is the epic dative plural of ἀγορή ‘assembly’. φραζομένῳ, a participle of φράζομαι ‘consider, plan’, agrees with μοι, and ἐσθλά is its object, ‘good things’.

sentences.t:
ἐπεὶ οὐδὲ μὲν οὐδὲ ἔοικε
δῆμον ἐόντα παρὲξ ἀγορευέμεν, οὔτ’ ἐνὶ βουλῇ
οὔτέ ποτ’ ἐν πολέμῳ, σὸν δὲ κράτος αἰὲν ἀέξειν·
sentences.tr:
epei oude men oude eoike
dēmon eonta parex agoreuemen, out’ eni boulēi
oute pot’ en polemōi, son de kratos aien aexein·
sentences.i: since it is not at all fitting for one of the people to speak out of line, either in council or ever in war, but always to increase your strength;
sentences.n: ἐπεὶ οὐδὲ μὲν οὐδὲ ἔοικε piles up negatives for emphasis, ‘it is not at all fitting’. δῆμον ἐόντα is ‘being (one) of the people’, an accusative because it goes with the infinitive ἀγορευέμεν. παρέξ means ‘outside, beyond’; whether ‘out of line’ is ‘against you’ or ‘out of turn’ the Greek does not say. οὔτ’ ἐνὶ βουλῇ οὔτέ ποτ’ ἐν πολέμῳ is ‘neither in council nor ever in war’. The last infinitive, ἀέξειν ‘to increase’, belongs to ἔοικε as well and is set against ἀγορευέμεν by δέ; κράτος is ‘strength’.

sentences.t: νῦν αὖτ’ ἐξερέω ὥς μοι δοκεῖ εἶναι ἄριστα.
sentences.tr: nyn aut’ exereō hōs moi dokei einai arista.
sentences.l: Now again I will speak out as it seems to me best.
sentences.i: Now once more I will speak out, as it seems to me best.
sentences.n: νῦν αὖτ’ ‘now again’ answers ἀεὶ μέν in 211. ἐξερέω is a future, ‘I will speak out’, from the stem ἐρ- that supplies the future of ‘say’. ὥς μοι δοκεῖ εἶναι ἄριστα is literally ‘as it seems to me to be best (things)’; δοκεῖ takes the dative μοι.

sentences.t: μὴ ἴομεν Δαναοῖσι μαχησόμενοι περὶ νηῶν.
sentences.tr: mē iomen Danaoisi machēsomenoi peri nēōn.
sentences.l: Let us not go to fight the Danaans about the ships.
sentences.i: Let us not go to fight the Danaans for the ships.
sentences.n: This is the advice itself, in six words. ἴομεν is the epic short-vowel subjunctive of εἶμι ‘go’, and with μή it forbids: ‘let us not go’. μαχησόμενοι is a future participle expressing purpose, ‘to fight’; the dative Δαναοῖσι is the people fought against. περὶ νηῶν is ‘about the ships’.

sentences.t: ὧδε γὰρ ἐκτελέεσθαι ὀΐομαι,
sentences.tr: hōde gar ekteleesthai oïomai,
sentences.l: For thus I suspect it will be fulfilled,
sentences.i: For I suspect it will be fulfilled in this way,
sentences.n: Polydamas gives his reading of the omen. ὧδε ‘thus’ looks ahead to the comparison that begins at 223. ἐκτελέεσθαι is the future infinitive of ἐκτελέω ‘fulfil’, with the uncontracted ending -έεσθαι. ὀΐομαι is ‘I suspect’, the word for an informed guess.

sentences.t:
εἰ ἐτεόν γε
Τρωσὶν ὅδ’ ὄρνις ἦλθε περησέμεναι μεμαῶσιν
αἰετὸς ὑψιπέτης ἐπ’ ἀριστερὰ λαὸν ἐέργων
φοινήεντα δράκοντα φέρων ὀνύχεσσι πέλωρον
ζωόν·
sentences.tr:
ei eteon ge
Trōsin hod’ ornis ēlthe perēsemenai memaōsin
aietos hypsipetēs ep’ aristera laon eergōn
phoinēenta drakonta pherōn onychessi pelōron
zōon·
sentences.l:
if truly
to the Trojans this bird came, as they were eager to cross,
a high-flying eagle, on the left keeping the people shut off,
bearing in its talons a blood-red serpent, a monster,
alive;
sentences.i: if in truth this bird came to the Trojans as they were eager to cross: a high-flying eagle, barring the army’s way on the left, carrying in its talons a blood-red serpent, a monster, alive;
sentences.n: εἰ ἐτεόν γε ‘if in truth’ makes the whole reading depend on the bird having come as a sign for the Trojans. Lines 218–220 repeat 200–202 apart from small changes (ἦλθε for ἐπῆλθε, Τρωσίν for σφιν, ὅδ’ ‘this’ added), and their English is kept; line 221 stops at ζωόν ‘alive’.

sentences.t:
ἄφαρ δ’ ἀφέηκε πάρος φίλα οἰκί’ ἱκέσθαι,
οὐδ’ ἐτέλεσσε φέρων δόμεναι τεκέεσσιν ἑοῖσιν.
sentences.tr:
aphar d’ apheēke paros phila oiki’ hikesthai,
oud’ etelesse pherōn domenai tekeessin heoisin.
sentences.l:
but straightway let it go before reaching its dear home,
and did not finish bearing it to give to its own children.
sentences.i: but at once it let it go before it could reach its dear home, and did not finish carrying it to give to its own children.
sentences.n: The subject is the eagle and the object is the serpent, left unstated. ἄφαρ ‘at once’; ἀφέηκε is the aorist of ἀφίημι in its uncontracted epic form. πάρος with the infinitive ἱκέσθαι means ‘before reaching’. οἰκί’ is οἰκία, ‘home’, neuter plural, with φίλα ‘dear’. ἐτέλεσσε (aorist of τελέω, with doubled σ) takes φέρων ‘bearing’ as a supplementary participle: it did not finish carrying. δόμεναι is the epic infinitive of δίδωμι ‘give’. ἑοῖσιν is the possessive ἑός ‘its own’, agreeing with τεκέεσσιν, the epic dative plural of τέκος ‘child’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἡμεῖς, εἴ πέρ τε πύλας καὶ τεῖχος Ἀχαιῶν
ῥηξόμεθα σθένεϊ μεγάλῳ, εἴξωσι δ’ Ἀχαιοί,
οὐ κόσμῳ παρὰ ναῦφιν ἐλευσόμεθ’ αὐτὰ κέλευθα·
sentences.tr:
hōs hēmeis, ei per te pylas kai teichos Achaiōn
rhēxometha stheneï megalōi, eixōsi d’ Achaioi,
ou kosmōi para nauphin eleusometh’ auta keleutha·
sentences.i: So it will be with us: even if we break the gates and the wall of the Achaeans with great strength, and the Achaeans give way, we shall not come away from the ships in good order, by the same paths;
sentences.n: ὣς ἡμεῖς ‘so (it will be) with us’ has no verb; the comparison is with the eagle that never got home. εἴ πέρ τε ‘even if’. ῥηξόμεθα and ἐλευσόμεθ’ are futures; εἴξωσι is the aorist subjunctive of εἴκω ‘give way’. σθένεϊ is the dative of σθένος ‘strength’. ναῦφιν is the epic ending -φιν with παρά, ‘from beside the ships’. οὐ κόσμῳ is ‘not in good order’, and αὐτὰ κέλευθα ‘the very same paths’ means the paths they came by.

sentences.t:
πολλοὺς γὰρ Τρώων καταλείψομεν, οὕς κεν Ἀχαιοὶ
χαλκῷ δῃώσωσιν ἀμυνόμενοι περὶ νηῶν.
sentences.tr:
pollous gar Trōōn kataleipsomen, hous ken Achaioi
chalkōi dēiōsōsin amynomenoi peri nēōn.
sentences.l:
for many of the Trojans we shall leave behind, whom the Achaeans
with bronze will cut down, defending themselves about the ships.
sentences.i: for we shall leave many of the Trojans behind, men whom the Achaeans will cut down with bronze as they defend themselves for the ships.
sentences.n: καταλείψομεν is the future of καταλείπω ‘leave behind’. οὕς κεν … δῃώσωσιν is a relative clause with the subjunctive, ‘whom (they) will cut down’; δῃόω is ‘cut down’, with χαλκῷ ‘with bronze’. ἀμυνόμενοι is ‘defending themselves’, and περὶ νηῶν is ‘about the ships’.

sentences.t:
ὧδέ χ’ ὑποκρίναιτο θεοπρόπος, ὃς σάφα θυμῷ
εἰδείη τεράων καί οἱ πειθοίατο λαοί.
sentences.tr:
hōde ch’ hypokrinaito theopropos, hos sapha thymōi
eideiē teraōn kai hoi peithoiato laoi.
sentences.l:
Thus would a diviner interpret, one who clearly in his heart
knew the portents, and whom the people would obey.”
sentences.i: So a diviner would interpret it, one who clearly knew the portents in his heart and whom the people would obey.”
sentences.n: ὧδέ χ’ ‘thus … would’ takes the optative ὑποκρίναιτο, ‘would interpret’; elsewhere ὑποκρίνομαι is ‘answer’, but of a sign it is to give its meaning. θεοπρόπος is a ‘diviner’, one who declares the will of the gods. εἰδείη and πειθοίατο are optatives in a relative clause, ‘one who knew’ and ‘whom they would obey’. σάφα ‘clearly’; τεράων is the genitive plural of τέρας ‘portent’, the thing known. This closes Polydamas’ speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν προσέφη κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ar’ hypodra idōn prosephē korythaiolos Hektōr·
sentences.l: Him then with a scowl looking addressed Hector of the glancing helmet:
sentences.i: Then Hector of the glancing helmet, looking at him with a scowl, spoke to him:
sentences.n: This is the usual line that brings in a reply, here with Hector of the glancing helmet; κορυθαίολος is κόρυς ‘helmet’ and αἰόλος ‘glancing’. The origin of ὑπόδρα ‘with a scowl’ is not certain. τὸν is ‘him’ (Polydamas); προσέφη is the aorist of προσφημί ‘address’.

sentences.t:
Πουλυδάμα, σὺ μὲν οὐκ ἔτ’ ἐμοὶ φίλα ταῦτ’ ἀγορεύεις·
οἶσθα καὶ ἄλλον μῦθον ἀμείνονα τοῦδε νοῆσαι.
sentences.tr:
Poulydama, sy men ouk et’ emoi phila taut’ agoreueis·
oistha kai allon mython ameinona toude noēsai.
sentences.l:
“Polydamas, you no longer say things dear to me;
you know how to devise also another speech, better than this.
sentences.i: “Polydamas, what you are saying is no longer dear to me; you know how to think of a better thing to say than this.
sentences.n: These two lines are the ones spoken to Antenor in an earlier part, with only the name changed (and οὐκ ἔτ’ printed as two words), and the English is kept. σὺ μὲν οὐκ ἔτ’ ‘you no longer’; φίλα ταῦτα is ‘things dear (to me)’. οἶσθα is the perfect of εἴδω, ‘you know’, with the infinitive νοῆσαι ‘to devise’; ἀμείνονα is the comparative ‘better’, with the genitive τοῦδε ‘than this’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἐτεὸν δὴ τοῦτον ἀπὸ σπουδῆς ἀγορεύεις,
ἐξ ἄρα δή τοι ἔπειτα θεοὶ φρένας ὤλεσαν αὐτοί,
ὃς κέλεαι Ζηνὸς μὲν ἐριγδούποιο λαθέσθαι
βουλέων, ἅς τέ μοι αὐτὸς ὑπέσχετο καὶ κατένευσε·
sentences.tr:
ei d’ eteon dē touton apo spoudēs agoreueis,
ex ara dē toi epeita theoi phrenas ōlesan autoi,
hos keleai Zēnos men erigdoupoio lathesthai
bouleōn, has te moi autos hypescheto kai kateneuse·
sentences.l:
But if truly indeed this you say in earnest,
then the gods themselves have utterly destroyed your wits,
you who urge us to forget the plans of loud-crashing Zeus,
which he himself promised me and nodded assent to;
sentences.i: But if you really are saying this in earnest, then the gods themselves have destroyed your wits, you who urge us to forget the plans of loud-crashing Zeus, which he himself promised me and nodded his assent to;
sentences.n: The first two lines repeat, word for word, a pair spoken earlier in the Iliad (it follows the lines to Antenor), but here they end in a comma and a relative clause follows, so the earlier English is kept up to the comma. ἐξ … ὤλεσαν (tmesis of ἐξόλλυμι) is ‘utterly destroyed’; ἀπὸ σπουδῆς ‘in earnest’. In ὃς κέλεαι (‘you who urge’) the Greek leaves the object unstated; λαθέσθαι takes the genitive βουλέων ‘plans’, and ἐριγδούποιο is ‘loud-crashing’. ἅς τέ μοι αὐτὸς ὑπέσχετο καὶ κατένευσε ‘which he himself promised me and nodded assent to’ comes from ὑπισχνέομαι ‘promise’, and κατένευσε from κατανεύω ‘nod assent’.

sentences.t:
τύνη δ’ οἰωνοῖσι τανυπτερύγεσσι κελεύεις
πείθεσθαι,
sentences.tr:
tynē d’ oiōnoisi tanypterygessi keleueis
peithesthai,
sentences.l:
but you bid us, to birds of omen, long-winged ones,
to give obedience,
sentences.i: but you bid us obey long-winged birds of omen,
sentences.n: τύνη is the epic form of σύ ‘you’, set against Zeus in the lines above. κελεύεις ‘you bid’ has its object (us) unstated, as at 235. πείθεσθαι ‘to obey’ takes the dative οἰωνοῖσι, ‘birds of omen’. τανυπτερύγεσσι is a dative plural of τανυπτέρυξ, ‘long-winged’ (τανυ- ‘stretched, long’ + πτέρυξ ‘wing’), a stock epithet of birds.

sentences.t:
τῶν οὔ τι μετατρέπομ’ οὐδ’ ἀλεγίζω
εἴτ’ ἐπὶ δεξί’ ἴωσι πρὸς ἠῶ τ’ ἠέλιόν τε,
εἴτ’ ἐπ’ ἀριστερὰ τοί γε ποτὶ ζόφον ἠερόεντα.
sentences.tr:
tōn ou ti metatrepom’ oud’ alegizō
eit’ epi dexi’ iōsi pros ēō t’ ēelion te,
eit’ ep’ aristera toi ge poti zophon ēeroenta.
sentences.l:
to which I do not at all turn my attention, nor care,
whether to the right they go, toward the dawn and the sun,
or to the left, they at least, toward the misty gloom.
sentences.i: I pay them no attention and do not care whether they go to the right, toward the dawn and the sun, or to the left, toward the misty gloom.
sentences.n: τῶν ‘of these’ is the genitive that goes with both verbs: μετατρέπομαι ‘turn my attention to’ and ἀλεγίζω ‘care for’. εἴτ’ … εἴτ’ is ‘whether … or’, with the subjunctive ἴωσι ‘they go’ (εἶμι). ἐπὶ δεξιά and ἐπ’ ἀριστερά are ‘to the right’ and ‘to the left’. The right is set toward dawn and the sun, the left toward ζόφος, the misty gloom, the dark quarter opposite the sunrise.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς δὲ μεγάλοιο Διὸς πειθώμεθα βουλῇ,
ὃς πᾶσι θνητοῖσι καὶ ἀθανάτοισιν ἀνάσσει.
sentences.tr:
hēmeis de megaloio Dios peithōmetha boulēi,
hos pasi thnētoisi kai athanatoisin anassei.
sentences.l:
but let us obey the plan of great Zeus,
who rules over all mortal men and immortals.
sentences.i: but let us obey the plan of great Zeus, who rules over all mortal men and immortals.
sentences.n: πειθώμεθα is a present subjunctive with the long vowel of epic, here urging: ‘let us obey’. It takes the dative βουλῇ ‘plan’. ὅς is the relative ‘who’. θνητοῖσι and ἀθανάτοισιν are dative plurals used as nouns, and ἀνάσσει takes the dative: ‘rules over’.

sentences.t: εἷς οἰωνὸς ἄριστος ἀμύνεσθαι περὶ πάτρης.
sentences.tr: heis oiōnos aristos amynesthai peri patrēs.
sentences.l: One bird of omen is best: to defend oneself about the fatherland.
sentences.i: One bird of omen is best: to defend one’s country.
sentences.n: This line is the heart of Hector’s answer: the only sign that counts is to fight for one’s country. εἷς ‘one’; οἰωνός is a bird of omen, here used figuratively. ἄριστος ‘best’ takes the infinitive ἀμύνεσθαι ‘to defend oneself’, and περὶ πάτρης is ‘about the fatherland’.

sentences.t: τίπτε σὺ δείδοικας πόλεμον καὶ δηϊοτῆτα;
sentences.tr: tipte sy deidoikas polemon kai dēïotēta;
sentences.l: Why ever do you fear war and fighting?
sentences.i: Why do you fear war and fighting?
sentences.n: τίπτε is τί ποτε ‘why ever’. δείδοικας is the perfect of δείδω ‘fear’, with a present sense. The pair πόλεμον καὶ δηϊοτῆτα ‘war and fighting’ also ended the last part (12.181).

sentences.t:
εἴ περ γάρ τ’ ἄλλοι γε περὶ κτεινώμεθα πάντες
νηυσὶν ἐπ’ Ἀργείων, σοὶ δ’ οὐ δέος ἔστ’ ἀπολέσθαι·
sentences.tr:
ei per gar t’ alloi ge peri kteinōmetha pantes
nēusin ep’ Argeiōn, soi d’ ou deos est’ apolesthai·
sentences.l:
For even if the rest of us are all killed round about
at the ships of the Argives, for you there is no fear of perishing;
sentences.i: For even if all the rest of us are killed at the ships of the Argives, you have no fear of perishing;
sentences.n: Hector turns the charge into an insult: Polydamas, he says, has nothing to fear, and the next line gives the reason. εἴ περ … κτεινώμεθα is a present subjunctive passive, ‘are killed’; περί is an adverb here, ‘round about’. νηυσὶν ἐπ’ Ἀργείων is ‘at the ships of the Argives’. δέος is ‘fear’, and ἀπολέσθαι the aorist infinitive of ἀπόλλυμαι ‘perish’.

sentences.t: οὐ γάρ τοι κραδίη μενεδήϊος οὐδὲ μαχήμων.
sentences.tr: ou gar toi kradiē menedēïos oude machēmōn.
sentences.l: for your heart is not foe-withstanding, nor fight-ready.
sentences.i: for your heart is not one to stand firm against the enemy, nor ready to fight.
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ ‘for … not’ gives the reason for the insult. κραδίη is ‘heart’. μενεδήϊος is a compound of μένω ‘stand firm’ and δήϊος ‘hostile’, so ‘one that stands firm against the enemy’; μαχήμων is ‘ready to fight’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δὲ σὺ δηϊοτῆτος ἀφέξεαι, ἠέ τιν’ ἄλλον
παρφάμενος ἐπέεσσιν ἀποτρέψεις πολέμοιο,
αὐτίκ’ ἐμῷ ὑπὸ δουρὶ τυπεὶς ἀπὸ θυμὸν ὀλέσσεις.
sentences.tr:
ei de sy dēïotētos aphexeai, ēe tin’ allon
parphamenos epeessin apotrepseis polemoio,
autik’ emōi hypo douri typeis apo thymon olesseis.
sentences.l:
But if you shall hold yourself away from fighting, or any other
man, having talked him over with words, you shall turn away from war,
at once, struck under my spear, you will lose your life.”
sentences.i: But if you hold yourself back from the fighting, or talk any other man round with words and turn him from the war, you will lose your life at once, struck by my spear.”
sentences.n: This is Hector’s threat. ἀφέξεαι is the future middle of ἀπέχω ‘hold off’, with the genitive δηϊοτῆτος ‘fighting’. παρφάμενος is an aorist middle participle meaning ‘talking round, winning over’, and ἀποτρέψεις (future, ‘you will turn away’) is its partner, with τιν’ ἄλλον ‘any other man’ the object of both: Polydamas will be killed if he does either. ὑπὸ δουρί with τυπείς (aorist passive participle of τύπτω ‘strike’) is ‘struck by my spear’. ἀπὸ … ὀλέσσεις is ‘you will lose’, with the verb split by tmesis; θυμόν is ‘life’, as in the phrase for a dying man’s life. This closes Hector’s speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἡγήσατο, τοὶ δ’ ἅμ’ ἕποντο
ἠχῇ θεσπεσίῃ·
sentences.tr:
hōs ara phōnēsas hēgēsato, toi d’ ham’ heponto
ēchēi thespesiēi·
sentences.l:
So then having spoken, he led the way, and they together followed
with wondrous din;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and led the way, and they followed along together with a wondrous din;
sentences.n: The first line is repeated word for word from the Odyssey (apart from the stop), and its English is kept. ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ‘so then having spoken’ closes the speech. ἡγήσατο is the aorist of ἡγέομαι ‘lead’; τοί is the old demonstrative ‘they’, which is turning into the article. ἕποντο is the imperfect of ἕπομαι. ἠχῇ θεσπεσίῃ is a dative of manner, ‘with wondrous din’.

sentences.t:
ἐπὶ δὲ Ζεὺς τερπικέραυνος
ὦρσεν ἀπ’ Ἰδαίων ὀρέων ἀνέμοιο θύελλαν,
sentences.tr:
epi de Zeus terpikeraunos
ōrsen ap’ Idaiōn oreōn anemoio thyellan,
sentences.l:
and upon them Zeus, delighting-in-the-thunderbolt,
roused from the Idaean mountains a storm-blast of wind,
sentences.i: and Zeus, who delights in the thunderbolt, roused a storm-blast of wind upon them from the mountains of Ida,
sentences.n: ἐπὶ δέ … ὦρσεν is a verb split by tmesis, ‘roused against (them)’; ὦρσεν is the aorist of ὄρνυμι. τερπικέραυνος is ‘delighting in the thunderbolt’. Ἰδαίων is the adjective ‘of Ida’ and ὀρέων the epic genitive plural of ὄρος ‘mountain’. θύελλα is the storm-blast, ἀνέμοιο ‘of wind’.

sentences.t: ἥ ῥ’ ἰθὺς νηῶν κονίην φέρεν·
sentences.tr: hē rh’ ithys nēōn koniēn pheren·
sentences.l: which straight toward the ships dust bore;
sentences.i: which carried the dust straight at the ships;
sentences.n: ἥ is the feminine relative ‘which’, agreeing with θύελλαν; ῥ’ is ῥα. ἰθύς is ‘straight’, with the genitive νηῶν ‘toward the ships’. φέρεν is the unaugmented imperfect of φέρω; κονίην is ‘dust’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιῶν
θέλγε νόον, Τρωσὶν δὲ καὶ Ἕκτορι κῦδος ὄπαζε.
sentences.tr:
autar Achaiōn
thelge noon, Trōsin de kai Hektori kydos opaze.
sentences.l:
but of the Achaeans
he was enchanting the mind, and to the Trojans and Hector glory he kept granting.
sentences.i: but he was enchanting the mind of the Achaeans, and kept granting glory to the Trojans and to Hector.
sentences.n: The subject is Zeus. αὐτὰρ marks the other half of what he does. θέλγε is the imperfect of θέλγω ‘enchant’; νόον is ‘mind’ (νόος). ὄπαζε is the imperfect of ὀπάζω ‘make follow, grant’; κῦδος is ‘glory’. The two imperfects stress that this goes on while the attack continues.

sentences.t:
τοῦ περ δὴ τεράεσσι πεποιθότες ἠδὲ βίηφι
ῥήγνυσθαι μέγα τεῖχος Ἀχαιῶν πειρήτιζον.
sentences.tr:
tou per dē teraessi pepoithotes ēde biēphi
rhēgnysthai mega teichos Achaiōn peirētizon.
sentences.l:
Trusting indeed in his portents and in might,
the great wall of the Achaeans to be broken they kept trying.
sentences.i: Trusting in his portents and in their might, they kept trying to break down the great wall of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: τοῦ is the pronoun ‘his’, Zeus’s: it takes up the portents he has shown. περ δή ‘indeed’; πεποιθότες is the perfect participle of πείθομαι, ‘trusting’, which takes the dative τεράεσσι ‘portents’ and βίηφι ‘might’ (the epic ending -φι marks the means). ῥήγνυσθαι is a passive infinitive, ‘to be broken’; the sense is that they sought to have the wall broken. πειρήτιζον is the imperfect of πειρητίζω ‘try’.

sentences.t: κρόσσας μὲν πύργων ἔρυον, καὶ ἔρειπον ἐπάλξεις,
sentences.tr: krossas men pyrgōn eryon, kai ereipon epalxeis,
sentences.l: The stepped ledges of the towers they were hauling down, and they were tearing down the battlements,
sentences.i: They were hauling down the stepped ledges of the towers and tearing down the battlements,
sentences.n: κρόσσας is the accusative plural of κρόσσαι; the word is rare, and what it names is not certain: some projecting, stepped part of the towers. μὲν … καί ties the two clauses. ἔρυον is the imperfect of ἐρύω ‘haul’, and ἔρειπον the imperfect of ἐρείπω ‘tear down’. ἐπάλξεις are the battlements, the screens along the top of the wall.

sentences.t:
στήλας τε προβλῆτας ἐμόχλεον, ἃς ἄρ’ Ἀχαιοὶ
πρώτας ἐν γαίῃ θέσαν ἔμμεναι ἔχματα πύργων.
sentences.tr:
stēlas te problētas emochleon, has ar’ Achaioi
prōtas en gaiēi thesan emmenai echmata pyrgōn.
sentences.l:
and the projecting pillars they were levering, which the Achaeans
first in the ground had set to be the supports of the towers.
sentences.i: and they were levering at the jutting pillars which the Achaeans had first set in the ground to be the supports of the towers.
sentences.n: στήλας is ‘pillars’; προβλῆτας ‘jutting out’ is the accusative plural of προβλής, from προβάλλω. ἐμόχλεον is the imperfect of μοχλέω ‘lever’ (μοχλός is a bar). ἃς ἄρ’ is ‘which indeed’. πρώτας agrees with ἃς: set ‘first’, that is at the base, before the rest. θέσαν is the aorist of τίθημι (= ἔθεσαν); ἔμμεναι is the epic ‘to be’, and ἔχματα ‘supports’ is from ἔχω.

sentences.t:
τὰς οἵ γ’ αὐέρυον, ἔλποντο δὲ τεῖχος Ἀχαιῶν
ῥήξειν·
sentences.tr:
tas hoi g’ aueryon, elponto de teichos Achaiōn
rhēxein·
sentences.l:
These they were hauling out, and they hoped the wall of the Achaeans
to break;
sentences.i: These they were hauling out, hoping to break the wall of the Achaeans;
sentences.n: τὰς is the pronoun ‘these’, taking up the pillars. αὐέρυον is the imperfect of αὐερύω ‘haul out’. ἔλποντο is the imperfect of ἔλπομαι ‘hope’; ῥήξειν is the future infinitive of ῥήγνυμι, the object being τεῖχος Ἀχαιῶν.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ νύ πω Δαναοὶ χάζοντο κελεύθου,
ἀλλ’ οἵ γε ῥινοῖσι βοῶν φράξαντες ἐπάλξεις
βάλλον ἀπ’ αὐτάων δηΐους ὑπὸ τεῖχος ἰόντας.
sentences.tr:
oude ny pō Danaoi chazonto keleuthou,
all’ hoi ge rhinoisi boōn phraxantes epalxeis
ballon ap’ autaōn dēïous hypo teichos iontas.
sentences.l:
and not yet were the Danaans giving ground from the path,
but they, with oxhides having fenced the battlements,
were striking from them the enemy going up under the wall.
sentences.i: And the Danaans were not yet giving ground from the path; they had fenced the battlements with oxhides and were striking from them at the enemy coming up under the wall.
sentences.n: οὐδέ νύ πω ‘and not yet’. χάζοντο is the imperfect of χάζομαι ‘give ground’, with the genitive κελεύθου ‘from the path’; which path is meant the poet does not say. ῥινοῖσι is the epic dative plural of ῥινός ‘hide’, and βοῶν ‘of oxen’ goes with it. φράξαντες is the aorist participle of φράσσω ‘fence’. ἀπ’ αὐτάων ‘from them’ means the battlements, and αὐτάων is the epic genitive plural feminine. δηΐους ‘the enemy’ takes the participle ἰόντας ‘going’, with ὑπὸ τεῖχος ‘up under the wall’. βάλλον is ‘were striking’ with missiles.

sentences.t:
ἀμφοτέρω δ’ Αἴαντε κελευτιόωντ’ ἐπὶ πύργων
πάντοσε φοιτήτην μένος ὀτρύνοντες Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
amphoterō d’ Aiante keleutioōnt’ epi pyrgōn
pantose phoitētēn menos otrynontes Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
And the two Ajaxes, both of them, giving orders on the towers
in every direction went to and fro, urging on the might of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: And the two Ajaxes, both of them, giving their orders, went to and fro along the towers in every direction, urging on the might of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: Dual forms mark the pair: ἀμφοτέρω Αἴαντε ‘both Ajaxes’, κελευτιόωντ’ ‘giving orders’ (a form of κελεύω, kept apart from ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’) and φοιτήτην ‘went to and fro’; the participle ὀτρύνοντες ‘urging on’ has the plural ending. ἐπὶ πύργων is ‘on the towers’, along which they go; πάντοσε is ‘in every direction’. μένος is ‘might’, here the fighting spirit of the Achaeans.

sentences.t:
ἄλλον μειλιχίοις, ἄλλον στερεοῖς ἐπέεσσι
νείκεον, ὅν τινα πάγχυ μάχης μεθιέντα ἴδοιεν·
sentences.tr:
allon meilichiois, allon stereois epeessi
neikeon, hon tina panchy machēs methienta idoien·
sentences.l:
one with gentle, another with hard words
they rebuked, whomever they saw altogether slackening from the fight:
sentences.i: They rebuked one man with gentle words and another with hard words, whomever they saw altogether slackening off from the fight:
sentences.n: ἄλλον … ἄλλον ‘one … another’ are the objects of νείκεον, the imperfect of νεικέω ‘rebuke’; μειλιχίοις and στερεοῖς ‘gentle’ and ‘hard’ go with ἐπέεσσι ‘words’. ὅν τινα … ἴδοιεν is an optative in a relative clause: ‘whichever man they saw’, on each occasion. πάγχυ is ‘altogether’; μεθιέντα is a participle of μεθίημι ‘slacken’, with the genitive μάχης ‘from the fight’.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι Ἀργείων ὅς τ’ ἔξοχος ὅς τε μεσήεις
ὅς τε χερειότερος,
sentences.tr:
ō philoi Argeiōn hos t’ exochos hos te mesēeis
hos te chereioteros,
sentences.l:
“O friends, of the Argives whoever stands out and whoever is middling,
and whoever is worse,
sentences.i: “Friends, whoever among the Argives stands out, whoever is middling, and whoever is worse,
sentences.n: ὦ φίλοι is ‘friends’ in address. Ἀργείων ‘of the Argives’ is the genitive that tells where the three ranks are found. ὅς τε … ὅς τε … ὅς τε is a generalising ‘whoever’ for each rank; ἔξοχος ‘standing out’, μεσήεις ‘middling’ and χερειότερος ‘worse’ (a comparative). The speech is addressed to the whole army and runs to the end of the part.

sentences.t:
ἐπεὶ οὔ πω πάντες ὁμοῖοι
ἀνέρες ἐν πολέμῳ, νῦν ἔπλετο ἔργον ἅπασι·
sentences.tr:
epei ou pō pantes homoioi
aneres en polemōi, nyn epleto ergon hapasi·
sentences.l:
since not yet are all alike, men, in war,
now there has come to be work for all;
sentences.i: since men are not all alike in war, now there is work for all;
sentences.n: ἐπεὶ οὔ πω … ὁμοῖοι: οὔ πω is literally ‘not yet’, but here it states a general truth, ‘not all men are alike’; ἀνέρες is the epic form of ἄνδρες. ἔπλετο is the aorist of πέλομαι, used like a present perfect, ‘has come to be’. ἔργον is ‘work’ and ἅπασι ‘for all’.

sentences.t: καὶ δ’ αὐτοὶ τόδε που γιγνώσκετε.
sentences.tr: kai d’ autoi tode pou gignōskete.
sentences.l: And indeed you yourselves, I suppose, recognise this.
sentences.i: And indeed you yourselves, I suppose, recognise this.
sentences.n: καὶ δ’ ‘and indeed’; αὐτοί ‘yourselves’ is emphatic. που is ‘I suppose’. γιγνώσκετε is ‘you recognise’. The unit ends at the full stop in the middle of line 272.

sentences.t:
μή τις ὀπίσσω
τετράφθω ποτὶ νῆας ὁμοκλητῆρος ἀκούσας,
sentences.tr:
mē tis opissō
tetraphthō poti nēas homoklētēros akousas,
sentences.l:
let no one backward
be turned toward the ships, having heard one who shouts at him,
sentences.i: let no one turn back toward the ships on hearing someone shout at him,
sentences.n: τετράφθω is the perfect passive imperative of τρέπω, ‘let him be turned’; μή τις ‘let no one’, and ὀπίσσω ‘backward’. ὁμοκλητῆρος is the genitive after ἀκούσας ‘having heard’: a ὁμοκλητήρ is one who shouts at another, and the Greek does not say whether he is friend or foe.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ πρόσω ἵεσθε καὶ ἀλλήλοισι κέλεσθε,
sentences.tr: alla prosō hiesthe kai allēloisi kelesthe,
sentences.l: but forward rush, and to one another urge,
sentences.i: but press forward and urge one another on,
sentences.n: πρόσω is ‘forward’. ἵεσθε is the present middle imperative of ἵημι, ‘send yourselves, rush’. κέλεσθε is the imperative of κέλομαι ‘urge’, with the dative ἀλλήλοισι ‘one another’.

sentences.t:
αἴ κε Ζεὺς δώῃσιν Ὀλύμπιος ἀστεροπητὴς
νεῖκος ἀπωσαμένους δηΐους προτὶ ἄστυ δίεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
ai ke Zeus dōēisin Olympios asteropētēs
neikos apōsamenous dēïous proti asty diesthai.
sentences.l:
if perhaps Zeus may grant, the Olympian, the lightning-flasher,
that we, having thrust off the quarrel, chase the enemy toward the town.”
sentences.i: if perhaps Zeus, the Olympian who flashes lightning, will grant that we thrust back the quarrel and drive the enemy to the town.”
sentences.n: αἴ κε … δώῃσιν ‘if perhaps (he) may grant’ is a hopeful clause, with the subjunctive. Ὀλύμπιος ἀστεροπητής is ‘the Olympian, the lightning-flasher’. δηΐους … δίεσθαι: the infinitive of δίεμαι ‘chase’ has the unstated subject ‘us’, which is why ἀπωσαμένους ‘having thrust off’ is accusative. νεῖκος ‘quarrel’ stands for the fighting. ἄστυ is ‘town’, here the Trojans’ own. This closes the Ajaxes’ speech and the part.
